newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin fails to end concern over nuclear button.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin fails to end concern over nuclear button.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's dilemma over giving up Russia's "nuclear button" while he has heart surgery has become a source of intense concern and speculation which the Kremlin has failed to dampen.
Despite his aides' newly declared policy of openness, details of how, when and to whom the 65-year-old president will transfer the main symbol of power in Russia remain hazy.

The constitution says Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin assumes the president's duties if Yeltsin is incapacitated. But it outlines no specific procedure for handing over the briefcase containing the trigger controlling Russia's nuclear missiles.

Yeltsin's spokesman said last week the president was considering whether to hand over power briefly and give up control of the nuclear button "around the time of the operation", but did not say to whom.
"Today the nuclear briefcase has become a symbol of power, just as the orb and sceptre once were," commercial NTV television's current affairs programme Itogi said on Sunday.
"Not only has no procedure (for handing over the nuclear button) been worked out, but no law has been written for it," correspondent Vadim Glusker said.
The lack of legal guidelines has fuelled speculation about Yeltsin's plans and why he has not made them clear.
Chernomyrdin has already won some temporary powers and appears almost certain to take over Yeltsin's role briefly when he has the bypass operation to improve blood flow to his heart.

Some commentators say Yeltsin could be delaying revealing his plans because of uncertainty over a power struggle between Chernomyrdin and security chief Alexander Lebed, although Lebed has said the premier should take brief charge.

Opposition communist leader Gennady Zyuganov has pounced on the delay, recounting a rumour that German Chancellor Helmut Kohl left with the nuclear button after a visit to Moscow earlier this month. Bonn and Moscow quickly denied this.
"From a political point of view, a person must take the necessary and correct decisions," Zyuganov told a news conference last Thursday.
"We want powers transferred to the prime minister in accordance with the law...This should have been done long ago instead of (Yeltsin) pretending to take decisions."
Yeltsin is not known to have handed over the "red button" before, but former Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev had it taken away briefly during the failed coup d'etat in August 1991.
Gorbachev signed a special decree handing the nuclear button to Yeltsin in 1991 when the Soviet Union collapsed.

Itogi quoted Kremlin sources as saying Yeltsin would sign a decree giving up the nuclear button just before his operation, the date of which has not yet been fixed. He would sign another decree to take it back as soon as his anaesthetic wore off.
Itogi also disclosed details about the chain of commands and coded messages in which the "nuclear button" is the first link and the firing of Russian nuclear missiles the final one.

When the authenticity of a presidential message is confirmed, duty officers open boxes with their own codes and send them to missile launching pads and nuclear submarines, defence expert and parliamentarian Alexei Arbatov told Itogi.
"Then the codes are installed, launch keys are turned and the missiles blast off," he said.
He said Defence Minister Igor Rodionov had a similar "nuclear button" but did not make clear whether he would need the president's authorisation to use it.
